The diamond turbot (Hypsopsetta guttulata) is a pleuronectiform flatfish endemic to the coastal waters of the eastern Pacific, ranging from northern California to the Gulf of California. Early life stages commence with the release of pelagic eggs following a spawning event, with each fertilised ovum measuring approximately 1.5 mm in diameter. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva emerges and relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase, a period during which the mouth is not yet functional. The wet weight at birth, based on the volume of an egg of this diameter, is estimated at 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value that reflects the modest size of the newly hatched larva. This initial mass is consistent with the small egg size typical of many coastal pleuronectids, which produce numerous, small propagules as part of a high-fecundity life-history strategy. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, a critical transition when the free-swimming larva must locate sufficient prey to sustain growth and avoid starvation.

Adult female diamond turbot exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters], a size that is attained after several years of sustained growth on soft-bottom habitats. This ultimate length is associated with a corresponding asymptotic wet weight of 2,780 grams [Wwi = 2,780 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for the species within the Pleuronectidae family. Individuals of this size are typically among the oldest and most reproductively active members of the population, dominating spawning aggregations in shallow sandy bays. Growth rates in this species show pronounced temperature dependence, with faster somatic development observed in the warmer southern portion of its geographic range. The relatively large body size achieved by females compared to conspecific males results from a combination of extended growth duration and a later onset of reproductive investment, allowing continued allocation of resources toward somatic mass accumulation well beyond the size at which males reach asymptotic dimensions.

Reproductive output in Hypsopsetta guttulata has been characterised through laboratory-based studies under controlled thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females are capable of producing approximately 2,466 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2,466 eggs per year], reflecting a high daily spawning rate that is sustained over the course of the breeding season. This daily fecundity translates into considerable annual reproductive potential, as individuals spawn repeatedly throughout the warmer months. The elevated temperature appears to accelerate both oocyte development and spawning frequency, consistent with the metabolic acceleration observed in many ectothermic teleosts under warmer regimes. This reproductive strategy, characterised by the continuous production of numerous small pelagic eggs, is typical of marine flatfishes that experience high larval mortality and rely on numerical abundance to ensure recruitment success. The daily rate at 25 °C represents the maximum reproductive output recorded for the species under optimal thermal conditions.

Longevity estimates for the diamond turbot are based on mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination conducted across its latitudinal range. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 3,285 days [am = 3,285 days] when assessed at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This value places Hypsopsetta guttulata among the longer-lived members of the Pleuronectidae, a family in which lifespans typically range from five to fifteen years depending on body size and environmental conditions. The relatively extended longevity is likely linked to the species' moderate growth rate and the absence of intensive fishing pressure across much of its range, allowing individuals to survive into advanced age classes. Older individuals often exhibit slower annual growth increments, with the greatest mass accumulation occurring during the first three to five years of life before reaching the asymptotic body size described previously. Temperature plays a critical role in determining the pace of senescence in this ectothermic flatfish.

The timing of sexual maturation in female diamond turbot has been established through histological examination of gonadal development in wild-caught specimens. At a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females reach puberty at approximately 912 days since birth [tp = approximately 912 days since birth], a value that corresponds to roughly two and a half years of age. This age at maturity is intermediate among pleuronectids of comparable body size, reflecting the energetic trade-off between continued somatic growth and the onset of reproductive activity. Maturation occurs when individuals have attained approximately half of their ultimate body length, a pattern commonly observed in flatfishes wherein a minimum size threshold must be reached before vitellogenesis and gametogenesis are initiated. The timing of this transition is influenced by local thermal regimes, with populations in warmer waters typically maturing earlier than those in cooler northern habitats. This pubertal schedule ensures that females are of sufficient size to support the high daily fecundity observed under optimal temperature conditions.
